title: SECTION A — ROLES, AUTHORITY AND MINDSET

questions.prompt: A therapist is appointed Driver. They tell the Passenger, “I am Driver, so I am senior for this session. Do not suggest anything.” What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing. Driver is a professional ranking above Passenger.
Driver and Passenger are session roles, not seniority. The Driver coordinates; the Passenger still thinks, observes, and may suggest.
The Passenger must remain silent unless the client complains.
Only a more-experienced therapist may ever be Driver.

questions.prompt: The Passenger is more experienced than the Driver. Mid-session they start giving continuous instructions, correcting every movement, and changing every decision. What has happened?
options: Correct mentorship. Experience automatically makes them Driver.
They are transferring skill the only way Zura allows: by taking over live.
Guidance has become takeover. They are guiding the Driver, not becoming the Driver. Many learning points belong in Therapist Review.
The Driver must surrender the session immediately because tenure always wins.

questions.prompt: A less-experienced Driver ignores a useful technique suggestion from an experienced Passenger because “I was appointed to lead.” What mindset is missing?
options: The Driver should reject all Passenger input to prove authority.
The Driver should abandon the role and let the Passenger drive unofficially.
Leadership includes using the Passenger’s knowledge. Rejecting useful input simply because it comes from the Passenger is not strong driving.
Suggestions are only allowed after the session, never during it.

questions.prompt: Two therapists start arguing about who is “in charge” while the client is on the table. What is the purpose of Driver–Passenger, and what is not?
options: The purpose is to decide who is professionally better.
The purpose is who controls whom.
The purpose is one coordinated massage: order, communication, skill transfer, and client experience — not a contest of superiority.
The purpose is for the Passenger to remain decorative while the Driver works alone.

questions.prompt: A Driver treats every Passenger suggestion as a challenge to their title. What does the standard say about this?
options: A Driver who cannot listen is not demonstrating strong leadership.
Listening removes the Driver’s authority, so they must refuse suggestions.
The Passenger should stop thinking so the Driver feels secure.
The Driver should announce they are Driver after every technique.

title: SECTION B — SESSION FLOW, QUALITY AND ROUTINES

questions.prompt: During Client Takeover, both therapists talk over each other, each trying to lead the client into the room. What should have happened?
options: Whoever is older should take over the greeting.
The Driver fully handles or initiates Takeover; the Passenger supports, observes, and assists without competing for the interaction.
The Passenger should always greet first so the Driver can watch.
Takeover is optional if the client has been before.

questions.prompt: During the hand and foot cleaning routine, where should each therapist work?
options: Whoever finishes first chooses any side.
Driver — right side of the client. Passenger — left side of the client. Both clean together according to the approved routine.
Only the Driver cleans; the Passenger waits.
Sides are swapped randomly so neither role is visible.

questions.prompt: The Driver says, “Calves are done,” and starts the next body part without checking with the Passenger, who still feels remaining tension. What rule was broken?
options: The Driver may never decide when to progress.
The Driver controls progression, but should not move on without reasonable confirmation from the Passenger. Both contribute to quality confirmation.
The Passenger must stay silent about remaining tension until Therapist Review.
Swapping sides is only for variety, so confirmation is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Why does Zura swap sides during a two-therapist session?
options: So therapists do not get bored.
So the Passenger can become Driver halfway through.
So each therapist can feel and assess the other’s work: remaining tension, side differences, pressure outcome, and whether more work is needed.
So the Driver can rest while the Passenger works alone.

questions.prompt: Warm compresses need replenishing. Both therapists are engaged, but one can step away with less disruption. Who should ordinarily handle setup, and why?
options: The Passenger must always do it because the role means errands.
The Driver must always leave, because they are in charge of equipment.
The person who can step away with the least disruption. Where practical, that is often the Passenger, so the Driver can keep session oversight — not because the Passenger is junior.
Neither should leave; skip the therapy rather than communicate.

title: SECTION C — COMMUNICATION, INITIATIVE AND LEARNING

questions.prompt: The Passenger feels remaining tension in a shoulder. Which communication matches the standard?
options: “No, that’s wrong. Let me lead.”
“You don’t know what you’re doing.”
“Driver, can we work this shoulder a little more? I’m still feeling tension here.”
Say nothing, then criticise the Driver after the client leaves.

questions.prompt: The Passenger wants to add a major hamstring stretch that would change the session sequence. What should they do first?
options: Start the stretch immediately; initiative never needs communication.
Communicate with the Driver first, for example: “Driver, I think a hamstring stretch would help here. Should we add it?”
Wait helplessly for the Driver to notice every small preparation task as well.
Announce the stretch to the client without involving the Driver.

questions.prompt: An experienced Passenger corrects a slightly inefficient (but safe and comfortable) technique throughout the entire session while the client is on the table. What should they have asked themselves?
options: “How do I prove I know more than the Driver?”
“Does this need to be corrected now, or can it be discussed during Therapist Review?” The client session is not a classroom.
“Should I remain completely silent even if the client is in pain?”
“Should I withhold the better technique forever because I am not driving?”

questions.prompt: A Passenger prepares oil and adjusts a stool without asking, then later changes treatment focus to another body area without telling the Driver. Which part was appropriate?
options: Both. All initiative is equal.
Neither. The Passenger may never act without permission.
Preparing materials and routine support may not need permission every time. Changing treatment focus or moving to another body area requires communication first. Initiative without chaos.
Changing body area is always Passenger-only; preparing oil always requires a meeting.

questions.prompt: An experienced Passenger withholds a stretch they know would help because “I’m not driving, so it’s not my job to teach.” What concern is this?
options: Correct role-boundary behaviour.
Teamwork concern. Skill transfer should depend on who currently has useful knowledge, not on who is senior or who is driving.
Required humility. Passengers must never share technique.
Proof that Driver training has failed.

title: SECTION D — SAFETY, ACCOUNTABILITY AND CLOSE

questions.prompt: The client is pulling away and grimacing. The Driver continues the same pressure. The Passenger can speak. What should they do?
options: Stay silent to protect the Driver’s ego.
Communicate immediately, for example: “Driver, the client appears uncomfortable. Can we reduce pressure?” Client safety and experience outrank protecting the Driver’s ego.
Escalate to management before saying anything to the Driver, even if a brief professional line would work.
Increase their own pressure to match the Driver so the session looks synchronized.

questions.prompt: The Driver refuses a suggestion about oil scent. The Passenger immediately escalates to leadership. Was that appropriate?
options: Yes. Every refused suggestion must be escalated.
No. Escalation is for genuine risk to safety, dignity, serious service quality, boundaries, or standards — not every minor disagreement.
Yes, because the Passenger is always right about products.
No, because Passengers may never escalate even if the client is unsafe.

questions.prompt: Client feedback is poor. The Driver immediately says, “It was the Passenger’s fault.” What does primary session accountability require instead?
options: The Driver should first be able to answer what they observed, decided, communicated, and whether they used the Passenger — not dump blame. The Passenger still remains accountable for their own misconduct.
The Passenger is never accountable for anything they did.
The Driver has no accountability if they were less experienced.
Poor feedback always means the appointment of Driver was invalid.

questions.prompt: There is conflict between the Driver’s preferred technique and a safety concern. Using the session decision hierarchy, what sits above Driver coordination?
options: Personal preference, then Passenger input, then the Driver.
Client safety; client dignity and boundaries; Zura Spa standard; client experience — all sit above Driver coordination.
Whoever has more years at Zura.
Whoever speaks more confidently.

questions.prompt: Management wants everyone to rotate as Driver this week. One therapist has not practised Takeover, Turnover, End Routine, reporting, or observation as Passenger. What does eligibility require?
options: They should drive immediately so rotation is fair.
Passing time at Zura is enough.
Driver status comes from readiness, not tenure. They should complete appropriate Passenger sessions, Driver training, and Driver assessment first.
They may drive only if the Passenger agrees to secretly lead.
